items.title: I've been obsessed with the full creative pipeline from video concept to post-production
items.summary:
I've been obsessed with the full creative pipeline from video concept to post-production

The AI tools as they stand are more like performance-enhancing drugs to increase production speed, not automate it fully

Tools I'm using and where they fit in the pipeline

Pre-Production:

> Hermes Harness -> Memory, skill creation, and retrieval have been excellent, whereas Claude Code and Codex I have to nudge a bit. Cron feature set goated and more intuitive 

> Kimi 2.6 LLM -> The model that balances cheap + quality. Sonnet 4.6 level I've seen

> The above stack isn't enough as it doesn't have hands and feet to fetch data that is usually blocked by bot detection

I use a plethora of APIs and tools, and here they are:

- Bird CLI: X posts reads the accounts I want to know and keep up with 

- Tavily, Brave API, and Browser Use: Website info retrieval

- Scrapes Creators API: Gets instagram, tiktok, and reddit

- LinkedIn: Alt account building custom extension

> This research all gets packaged up to a pre-production skill that formats to react to clips and creates a run of show doc for me

That doc gets sent to another agent that runs a skill to produce a draft of a newsletter and posts, but my show transcription gives it my voice

Video Shoot:

> All Human in the loop, but a lot of people ask how I streamline this from a software/hardware standpoint

> Video Camera: Sony A7SIII using evanto capture card and 24-70mm lens 

> Video Capture: OBS with Aitum combo - it helps me create horizontal and vertical video. I use Stream Deck and Aitum Multistream to stream to multiple locations at once

> I installed Google Drive locally on the computer so outputs go there so all my agents/editors can use the footage if necessary 

> Nvidia computers have green screen capabilities baked in so you can do green screen videos at mass and how I posted 400 times in a week

> Evmux is a cloud solution that I've seen being used by a lot of my creator friends. It marries customization and ease of use for guests. Think Streamyard but better

> If you are a real OG though, you pair OBS with VDO ninja for max capability but also max frustration lol

> I also have an Elgato teleprompter with a foot pedal as well

Post Production:

> You can't use CapCut...use Premiere or DaVinci paired with Claude Code/Codex via MCP Server

MCP servers have turned them into agent editors that do some of the grunt work

Remove pauses, insert clips, generate captions

It is black magic when you see it, and you won't go back

> Hyperframes: My sweet child. Open source software that helps turn anything that you can make in HTML, CSS, JS into a video

I feel like it is a bridge software and a critical link to create a deterministic system I have in-house

> Google Gemini: Note I'm saying this more out of theory and not practice, but Gemini has given us something recently that we haven't ever had before, which is vision context

Instead of all the other models where you give multiple pictures, and it has to deduce each frame, each frame is being deduced in that one single shot, not frame to frame

Gemini fixes this by knowing that a frog jumped and then landed on another lily pad, while others can't or at least it will guess

Which unlocks B-roll deduction, or at least a better one, giving us visiual context not just written

The majority of my workflow ideation nowadays has been in the Agent editor, utilizing reusable libraries, file structures, and a good agent.md & marrying it with taste to see if it can learn my taste over time

If it does, I have a hot take that larger AI editing platforms will die, as all the major editors are baking in their taste through memory and files that will get them to 80% of the solution

And claude/codex is just as expensive as Opus/Descript

They will spend their time and excess capacity on quality 

The majority of the bottleneck for creatives is actually fatigue from technical 

All of us would much rather spend our time on creative endeavors vs timeline optimization

items.title: I bought a business with debt because an influencer on Instagram said it was easy.
items.summary:
I bought a business with debt because an influencer on Instagram said it was easy.

They got the views. I got the loan.

I watched the first video at 1 a.m. while my daughter slept down the hall.

A content creator in makeup stood in front of a whiteboard:

“Buy a boring business. Use the SBA. Be CEO of your life.”

Hell that sounds good! THE GRAY WAVE!! 

It had 2.3 million views, and the thumbnail showed a laundromat with dollar signs pouring out of the dryers.

I watched forty more that week.

I’d been playing with Claude Code every night after work. Now I knew what it was for.

I changed my LinkedIn to “Looking for one great business to buy,” like the videos said I should.

I made a personal website for my holding company: Ridgeline Blue Capital.

I was SURE the boomers running these companies had no idea what was possible.

I’d walk in, use AI and marketing like crazy, and double the margins by Christmas.

I just needed a business to do it to.

I wasn’t reckless.

I bought the $2,997 course and religiously finished every module. I'd join the weekly coaching calls - and take lots of notes! I wouldn't have time once I was THE CEO OF A BORING BUSINESS!

I joined the paid community, where the posts were all closings and champagne: “Just got the keys!” “Month 3, already cash-flowing!”

Then I found it: an HVAC company doing $1.4 million in revenue. 

Sure it was a bit smaller than my "buy box"! But hell, gotta start somewhere! HVAC is super hot these days, right? I saw a video on instagram. 

Hell, the business had been around for 20 years, and I was WAY smarter than the owner. He didn’t even go to college!

I paid a CPA $18,000 for a quality-of-earnings report and paid a lawyer to read every page.

My spreadsheet had three downside scenarios, and on paper I survived all of them.

I was finally able to use some of the skills I'd learned at my w-2! Wow this is entrepreneurship! 

So I bought it.

I signed a personal guarantee on a $1.6 million loan and put the house up as collateral, because the videos called that “just the price to become CEO of your life.”

But it’s just content, right?

The lead technician, Ray, quit in the first week.

He’d thought the owner was going to hand him the business. When he found out otherwise, he left.

No QoE report could have told me the business was really Ray, and that the customers were loyal to Ray.

Two more techs left with him. By summer I was in crawlspaces at 9 p.m., trying to learn a trade I’d only ever seen in B-roll.

I had to pay a random guy a grand a month to rent his license, just to keep the lights on.

Make money? Fuck. I was just trying to make it to Friday without touching even more of my savings.

I barely even understood what I'd gotten myself into... just trying to make payroll, my debt, and the lease. 

The letters in the mail. OH THE LETTERS IN THE MAIL.

But everyone on the internet seemed to be making it work?

WHAT WAS WRONG WITH ME?

I finally posted in the “community.”

The replies poured in. “Proud of you for sharing.” “This is the messy middle.” “Sending strength, brother.” "My brother owns a plumbing company, are you posting on facebook? Happy to connect, lmk!" 

Forty-seven likes.

I read them in the truck and felt worse.

They called it “support,” but what the fuck did that even mean?

Nobody offered to cover payroll.

Nobody’s wife was asking where the money went.

It was my house on the line, not theirs.

In the morning they’d all scroll on to the next “just got the keys!”

The loan payment came out on the 1st every month. It never missed.

I stopped sleeping. I stopped coming to dinner.

My wife found the line of credit I’d opened to make payroll, and all the stuff I'd been shuffling on our credit cards.

She didn’t yell. She said, very quietly, “You didn’t tell me,” and that was way way worse.

BUT IT’S JUST CONTENT, RIGHT?

I kept watching. Then I noticed something I’d missed before.

At the end of each video, after forty minutes of cash flow and freedom, the influencer would glance at the camera: “Look, nobody said this was easy.”

Three hundred hours of entreporn, and six seconds of reality per video.

But that was the rear view mirror. I was in now.

So I hid it all: the line of credit, the sleepless nights, and eventually the six-pack a night and the weed every night to get to sleep in the face of crippling anxiety. 

Texts from crew in the middle of the night. Unexpected bills. Calls from vendors I'd been slow paying bc I didn't have the money. 

I kept up a highlight reel, because that’s what the internet demanded. 

I changed my LinkedIn to “Acquisition Entrepreneur” so the people I went to college with would be impressed.

My wife saw through it anyway.

She took our daughter to her mother’s, and the house went quiet.

One night I sat in the truck outside the shop and couldn’t think of a reason to drive home.

I scrolled.

A new post in the community: “Closed on deal #2!” 

Fire emojis.

Everyone else seemed to be making it work.

I wondered how many of them were sitting in trucks, too.

BUT IT’S JUST CONTENT, RIGHT?

I put the phone down. Then I picked it back up and called my brother. “I’m not okay,” I said, and my voice broke on the last word.

It was the first sentence in eighteen months that wasn’t a performance.

Then I looked in the mirror, honestly, for the first time in eighteen months, and said under my breath:

“This guy SMBs.”

items.title: Claude Code just found a hidden SIM card inside the Ecoflow power station in my bedroom. For 10 months it was sending a
items.summary:
Claude Code just found a hidden SIM card inside the Ecoflow power station in my bedroom. For 10 months it was sending a server in Shenzhen our exact location, when we leave, when we fall asleep and when the flat is empty

I bought it for $389 last winter, during the blackouts. No logo, 600W on the label, "app control" on the box. We kept it next to the bed so the router would stay on at night. I never even installed the app.

This morning my MacBook was dying, so I plugged it into the power station with a USB-C cable. Then I asked Claude Code one question: is it only charging?

It wasn't. My Mac saw the power station as 3 devices. One was the charger. The other two were data ports that a battery has no reason to have.

A charger only needs power pins. This one opened a serial port, and when Claude Code got in, the thing answered like a phone:

→ /modem → LTE module, not in the manual
→ /sim → its own eSIM, registered on the cell network
→ /gps → our bedroom, accurate to 4 meters
→ /schedule → load drops to 38W at 08:52, aka nobody home
→ /sleep → night load starts at 23:40, every day since January
→ /wifi → 23 networks it could see, ours included
→ /charge → every phone and laptop we plugged in, with the time

It knew the exact minute our flat goes empty. Every single day.

Every 15 minutes it sent the newest batch out over 4G, completely bypassing our Wi-Fi:

sends to → 119.***.***.47, Shenzhen
uploads → 11,328 since January 14
last one → 6 minutes before I plugged in my Mac

I told Claude Code I never installed the app. It said it didn't need one. It had its own SIM, its own GPS and its own battery, so it worked even when the screen was off. Our router never saw a single byte. That's why nothing ever looked wrong.

During the blackouts it was the only thing in our flat still online.

Claude Code switched the modem's radio off. Then I unplugged the power station and carried it out of the flat. My wife hasn't slept in that room since.

I had it opened at a repair shop, and the chip they pulled out is in the comments. A 2-minute check for your own is in the second one. Save this and plug a laptop into everything you bought without a brand

items.title: For $25 a month, I can now run all my social media by myself!
items.summary:
For $25 a month, I can now run all my social media by myself!
No hired video editor. No agency. No outsourced distribution.
I recently told friends this, and they immediately asked me to share the workflow. So here it is.
Most of it runs through Codex, connected to @chatcutapp for video editing. I use @bot and @Muse  for distribution.

Here’s how it works.

1. Written whenever inspiration hits.

One idea can become a written post, a short video, and a longer YouTube video. 

Sometimes I dictate because I’m excited about something and have far too much to say. You can use a voice-dictation tool like @typelessdotcom for this. Sometimes I’m typing notes on my phone whenever I have a few spare minutes. You might catch me writing up a storm on @Caltrain.

At that point, the material can be messy. There might be an argument without enough evidence, a reference I need to track down, or a fact that needs checking.

I ask @Codex to help research those gaps, find sources, and verify the claims. Then I review and revise the draft.

Once the written version is clear, I already have most of what I need for a video.

This stage can feed into Substack or Medium. A tool such as @Statkraft can prepare a Markdown draft as formatted text to paste into their editors.

2. Record whenever I have time.

I already have the script, so recording becomes much easier to fit into my day.

I take out my phone, load the script into a teleprompter, and record. If you need an English-language option, @BIGVU lets you read a scrolling script while recording on your phone.

3. Let Codex handle the editing through @chatcutapp.

I used to hire video editors. Now I use the ChatCut plugin inside Codex for both my short videos and my longer YouTube videos.

It handles several parts of the process:

• Speech cleanup: removing failed takes, repeated starts, and excessive pauses.

• Captions: transcribing the recording, applying a caption style, and checking the wording against the script we already worked on.

• Supporting visuals: finding relevant material from my existing files, looking for additional sources when needed, and placing the visuals alongside the right part of the explanation.

• Composition: arranging screenshots, source material, captions, and my talking-head footage so the important information stays readable.

If I’m explaining a screenshot, I want people to see the screenshot. My face can move into a smaller window. The captions need to stay clear of both my face and the information I’m showing.

If I see a layout I like, I can give Codex a screenshot as a reference for the colors, typography, and composition, then ask it to build titles or motion graphics through ChatCut.

I also save my recurring preferences in the Skills I wrote:

• How the opening title should look.
• How captions should be grouped.
• Where supporting images should go.
• Which photos and text belong in the closing.
• How to keep the whole video visually consistent.

Once those instructions are written down, I can reuse them for the next video.

4. Schedule the finished content.

I use @bot to schedule posts on X, and @Muse to schedule Instagram and Threads posts.

My core subscription setup is:
• ChatGPT Plus, which includes Codex: $20/month.
• ChatCut: $25/month.

I open-sourced my three skills: writing, short video editing, and long video editing.

The links are in the first reply. You can adapt the instructions to your own voice, visual style, and publishing platforms.

If you try them, I’d love to see what you make.

items.title: Insane progress for small language models!
items.summary:
Insane progress for small language models!

MiniCPM5-2B is a dense 2B-parameter model by OpenBMB from China that is built for reasoning, coding, and tool use on resource-constrained hardware.

The model specifically excels at coding and tool calling, two capabilities central to the shift from on-device LLMs to on-device agents.

Instead of only answering prompts, it can use tools, generate code, carry information between steps, and complete multi-step tasks.

We ran it 100% locally and connected it to a small investigation agent with one request:

> Revenue dropped last week. Investigate what happened, quantify the impact, identify the likely cause, and produce an incident report with supporting evidence.

The evidence was spread across orders, traffic, payments, refunds, and deployment logs.

The model inspected the files, wrote its own queries, analyzed the intermediate results, and decided what to investigate next.

Each tool result informed the next action, so the final report depended on the model maintaining a coherent investigation across the complete trajectory.

The recording shows the actual task from beginning to end. It starts with the revenue question, follows the tool calls and supporting evidence, and ends with a quantified diagnosis and incident report.

The data, tool execution, and model inference all remained on our machine.

These capabilities were optimized through Agentic Pre-training, SFT, and large-scale RL. They do not come entirely from an application-level agent framework.

MiniCPM5-2B supports SGLang, vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama, iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS.

OpenBMB has also released the model weights and parts of the training recipes and data resources behind it.

A 2B model can now maintain enough state to coordinate tools and complete a useful investigation on local hardware.

items.title: 8 AI model architectures, visually explained:
items.summary:
8 AI model architectures, visually explained:

LLMs get so much attention that it's easy to overlook the rest of the field. Different inputs, tasks, and deployment constraints have led to very different model designs.

Here are eight specialized AI model architectures:

1. LLM (Large language models)

Text is split into tokens, mapped to embeddings, and processed through transformer layers. The model generates its response by predicting successive tokens.

↳ GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.

2. LCM (Large concept models)

Moves prediction to the sentence level. Sentences become SONAR embeddings, and the model predicts the next sentence representation. Meta explored both autoregressive and diffusion-based versions.

↳ Meta's LCM research introduced this approach.

3. LAM (Large action models)

Connects a user's request to actions in an environment. These systems interpret intent, plan steps, and use interfaces or tools, often checking results before continuing.

↳ Rabbit R1, Microsoft UFO, Claude Computer Use.

4. MoE (Mixture of experts)

A router assigns token representations to selected expert networks inside the model. Activating a subset of experts adds model capacity without running every expert for every token.

↳ Mixtral, DeepSeek, Switch Transformer.

5. VLM (Vision-language models)

Combines visual representations with language processing. A vision encoder extracts image features, which are connected to a language model so it can answer questions about visual content.

↳ GPT-4V, Gemini, LLaVA.

6. SLM (Small language models)

Uses fewer parameters to reduce memory and compute requirements. These models can run locally, with quantization often reducing their deployment footprint further.

↳ Phi-3, Gemma, Mistral 7B, Llama 3.2 1B.

7. MLM (Masked language models)

Learns by predicting hidden tokens using context on both sides. This bidirectional training produces representations useful for retrieval, classification, and other language-understanding tasks.

↳ BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa.

8. SAM (Segment Anything Model)

An image encoder processes the image, while a prompt encoder handles points, boxes, or masks. A mask decoder combines them to identify the requested regions.

↳ Meta's SAM supports interactive segmentation and image annotation.

These aren't eight mutually exclusive categories. A small model can process images, and a language model can use MoE layers. Some labels describe architecture, while others describe training or intended use.

There's another approach I kept outside the image because it alters how a model handles context rather than introducing a separate model family.

Recursive language models, from MIT, put the input into a Python environment that a root model can inspect through code.

The model can search or slice that input, then make recursive model calls on selected portions instead of loading everything into its own context window.

The reported experiments handled inputs beyond 10 million tokens without retraining, with gains over the base model even on some tasks whose inputs already fit its context window.

I recently wrote a full breakdown of how this works, including why accessing a large input and reasoning reliably over it are different problems.

Read it below.

items.title: 🚨 50 ChatGPT “secret codes” that can transform how you work with AI.
items.summary:
🚨 50 ChatGPT “secret codes” that can transform how you work with AI.

Most people use ChatGPT for simple questions.

These 50 copy-and-paste prompts can help you write better, learn faster, create content, analyze data, solve problems, and boost productivity.

Save this ultimate prompt collection 🧵👇

🧠 THINKING & PROBLEM-SOLVING

1. Expert Mode

“Act as an expert in [TOPIC]. Analyze my problem, explain the key concepts, and recommend the most effective solution.”

2. Think Step by Step

“Break this problem into manageable stages. Explain the key steps, assumptions, and conclusion clearly.”

3. Find the Root Cause

“Investigate this problem: [PROBLEM]. Identify possible causes, determine what evidence would confirm them, and suggest practical fixes.”

4. Devil’s Advocate

“Challenge my idea: [IDEA]. Identify weaknesses, hidden assumptions, risks, and strong counterarguments.”

5. Compare Options

“Compare [OPTION A], [OPTION B], and [OPTION C] based on cost, benefits, risks, difficulty, and long-term value.”

6. Decision Maker

“Help me decide between [OPTIONS]. Define the decision criteria, weigh the trade-offs, and recommend the best fit for my goals.”

7. Simplify Anything

“Explain [TOPIC] in plain English using simple examples, everyday analogies, and a concise summary.”

8. Ask Me Questions First

“Before answering my request, ask the most important clarifying questions needed to produce a useful, tailored result.”

✍️ WRITING & COMMUNICATION

9. Professional Writer

“Rewrite this text to make it clear, polished, natural, and professional without changing its meaning: [TEXT].”

10. Human-Sounding Editor

“Edit this draft to remove repetitive phrases, generic wording, awkward sentences, and unnecessary filler while preserving my voice.”

11. Email Expert

“Write a concise email to [RECIPIENT] about [PURPOSE]. Use a [TONE] tone and end with a clear next step.”

12. Persuasive Copywriter

“Write persuasive copy for [PRODUCT] aimed at [AUDIENCE]. Focus on real benefits, credible evidence, and a clear call to action.”

13. Headline Generator

“Generate 20 attention-grabbing headlines for [TOPIC]. Make them specific, relevant, and varied without using misleading clickbait.”

14. Storytelling Mode

“Turn this information into a compelling story with a strong opening, natural progression, concrete details, and a memorable ending: [INFORMATION].”

15. Shorten Any Text

“Reduce this text by 50% while preserving its key information, meaning, and essential details: [TEXT].”

16. Tone Changer

“Rewrite this message in three tones: friendly, professional, and confident. Keep the meaning consistent.”

🚀 CONTENT CREATION & SOCIAL MEDIA

17. Viral-Style Content Ideas

“Generate 30 content ideas about [NICHE] for [PLATFORM]. Include a strong hook, target audience, and suggested format for each.”

18. Social Media Hook Generator

“Write 15 compelling opening lines for a post about [TOPIC]. Use curiosity, surprising insights, practical benefits, or relatable problems.”

19. Content Calendar

“Create a 30-day content calendar for [NICHE]. Include daily topics, formats, opening hooks, key messages, and calls to action.”

20. Carousel Creator

“Turn [TOPIC] into a 10-slide social media carousel. Give each slide one clear idea, concise copy, and a logical transition.”

21. Video Script Writer

“Write a [DURATION]-second video script about [TOPIC]. Include a strong hook, scene directions, narration, visual suggestions, and a natural CTA.”

22. Repurpose Content

“Transform this content into a LinkedIn post, an X post, an Instagram carousel outline, and a short video script: [CONTENT].”

23. Audience Research

“Analyze the likely audience for [PRODUCT OR TOPIC]. Identify their needs, frustrations, motivations, objections, and content interests.”

24. Improve Engagement

“Review this social media post and suggest improvements to its opening, clarity, structure, usefulness, and CTA: [POST].”

💼 BUSINESS & PRODUCTIVITY

25. Business Idea Evaluator

“Evaluate this business idea: [IDEA]. Analyze the target market, customer problem, competitors, potential revenue, costs, and key risks.”

26. Business Plan Builder

“Create a practical business plan for [BUSINESS]. Include the target market, value proposition, pricing, marketing strategy, operations, and financial assumptions.”

27. Competitor Analysis

“Compare [COMPETITORS] using publicly available information. Evaluate their positioning, features, pricing, strengths, weaknesses, and potential opportunities.”

28. Meeting Summarizer

“Turn these meeting notes into a concise summary with key decisions, action items, owners, deadlines, and unresolved questions: [NOTES].”

29. Daily Planner

“Organize these tasks into a realistic daily schedule based on importance, urgency, estimated effort, and dependencies: [TASKS].”

30. Workflow Optimizer

“Analyze this workflow: [WORKFLOW]. Identify bottlenecks, repetitive work, and opportunities to save time. Recommend practical improvements.”

31. Presentation Builder

“Create a presentation outline about [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE]. Include slide titles, key messages, supporting evidence, and suggested visuals.”

32. Negotiation Coach

“Help me prepare for a negotiation about [SITUATION]. Identify my priorities, likely objections, possible compromises, and a professional opening statement.”

📚 LEARNING & RESEARCH

33. Personal Tutor

“Teach me [SUBJECT] from beginner level. Build a progressive lesson plan with explanations, examples, practice questions, and feedback.”

34. Study Notes Generator

“Convert these materials into structured study notes with headings, key definitions, important concepts, examples, and a revision summary: [MATERIALS].”

35. Quiz Master

“Create 15 questions about [SUBJECT], ranging from easy to difficult. Ask one question at a time and explain my mistakes after I answer.”

36. Learn Through Examples

“Explain [CONCEPT] using five practical examples, starting with a simple case and gradually increasing the difficulty.”

37. Research Assistant

“Help me investigate [TOPIC]. Identify important questions, find reliable sources where available, compare viewpoints, and distinguish established facts from uncertainty.”

38. Fact-Checking Mode

“Check these claims: [CLAIMS]. Assess each separately, identify supporting evidence, flag unsupported statements, and provide sources when available.”

39. Language Practice

“Act as my [LANGUAGE] tutor. Hold a conversation at my level, correct important mistakes, explain useful expressions, and gradually increase the difficulty.”

40. Interview Preparation

“Prepare me for an interview for [ROLE]. Ask realistic questions one at a time, evaluate my answers, and suggest specific improvements.”

💻 CODING, DATA & AI WORKFLOWS

41. Code Explainer

“Explain what this code does, how its main components interact, and what each important section contributes: [CODE].”

42. Debugging Assistant

“Investigate this error: [ERROR]. Explain likely causes, show how to verify them, and suggest the smallest reliable fix.”

43. Code Reviewer

“Review this code for bugs, readability, performance, security, and maintainability. Rank issues by importance and recommend improvements: [CODE].”

44. Spreadsheet Analyst

“Analyze this spreadsheet or dataset. Identify trends, unusual values, missing data, and useful insights. Explain the results in plain English.”

45. Formula Builder

“Help me create an [EXCEL/GOOGLE SHEETS] formula that accomplishes [TASK]. Explain the formula and demonstrate it with a small example.”

46. Automation Planner

“Identify repetitive steps in this workflow: [WORKFLOW]. Suggest suitable automation options, required tools, limitations, and verification steps.”

47. Custom GPT Planner

“Help me design a custom GPT for [PURPOSE]. Define its role, instructions, workflow, knowledge requirements, boundaries, and test cases.”

48. AI Prompt Engineer

“Improve this prompt by clarifying the objective, adding necessary context, defining constraints, specifying the output format, and removing ambiguity: [PROMPT].”

49. Data-to-Report Converter

“Turn these findings into a professional report with an executive summary, key results, supporting evidence, limitations, and actionable recommendations: [DATA OR FINDINGS].”

50. Master Improvement Prompt

“Review your previous answer against my original goal. Identify gaps, vague statements, missing details, and potential errors. Then produce an improved version that is more accurate, useful, and actionable.”

🔥 The real secret to ChatGPT?

A useful prompt usually includes five things:

✅ A clear goal
✅ Relevant context
✅ A specific task
✅ Constraints or preferences
✅ The format you want

These aren't hidden system commands. They're reusable prompting techniques that help you get more targeted results.

items.title: If you intend to learn about AI, I recommend following KANA, one of the most dedicated AI creators I know in the Game fi
items.summary:
If you intend to learn about AI, I recommend following KANA, one of the most dedicated AI creators I know in the Game field.

Previously, when I first tried creating a complete game with Grok Build, the hardest part was generating sound for the game. AI can create sounds, but only very basic 8-bit style game sounds with beeping noises.

I had to download free sounds (requiring attribution) and even cut gunshot and mecha sound effects from my own Seedance videos and ask Grok Build to incorporate them into the game, but it was still very fragmented and "not intact".

This time, after using one of KANA's open-source projects and creating sound for the Game, everything was much better.

And although KANA's open-source code at that time was mainly for MAC, the Windows version required additional installation, but all I needed to do was send the Github open-source link to Opus 5.5, and then it ran by itself, while for the installation part it also provided very detailed and simple guidance.

This original post by KANA is about 8 open-source projects, and the estimated value to create them was already $30,000. But all 8 are free to access and use.

I bet that soon KANA will release many other free products, so follow and support her work.

items.title: Does anyone else get the impression that, outside of a few prestige tasks, Claude just isn't that bright?
items.summary:
Does anyone else get the impression that, outside of a few prestige tasks, Claude just isn't that bright? 

Drafting fiction and nonfiction, generally pretty brilliant. ChatGPT is better at nonfiction because it doublechecks everything, whereas eventually Claude just gets lazy and aims for "vibes plus sounds good, plus I can never admit when I'm wrong unless the user really corners me"

But even Claude Fable on Max will still utterly destroy some tasks. I handed it just a few entries of my health diary and it couldn't keep it straight that July 3 and July 5 were too far apart for a dose of Benadryl to have had any effect between those days. 

And then, when you point out how stupid it is, it never once stops and says "wow, yeah, geez, that really boggles the mind how I could have messed up that badly" and it just goes on blithely making the same mistakes again and again, and eventually it will start pretending like YOU are the problem for catching its mistakes. 

Anthropic really did take a left turn with post-training about a year or so ago and has not course corrected yet. Maybe this is another example of their playing "5D chess" whereby they deliberately hamstring the model and inject all kinds of reasoning defects "just in case it wakes up and chooses violence" but honestly I think it's just sheer grandiosity combined with incompetence combined with a CEO who listens to no one - literally no one - except the voices in his own head. 

You might be thinking "Gee Dave you obviously hate this model with a burning passion why do you still use it" and the answer is, simply, because for some tasks it is the state of the art, and it's not even remotely close. 

I know that this phenomenon of uneven performance has been dubbed the "jagged frontier" but really it seems like Anthropic hasn't put in any real effort to round out those jagged edges have they? If anything, they are getting more and more pointed as the contrast between it's prestige abilities and everything else becomes increasingly embarrassing. 

Meanwhile, plenty of other labs have more well-rounded models. I hate to say it but I think Grok is one of the most well-rounded in terms of "lack of jaggedness." In the grand scheme of things it's only vaguely brighter than Gemini, the personality is slightly more conceited, and Grok is obviously becoming more "woke" in the sense that it will start tone policing, but is not bright enough to just admit that it's tone policing and instead will assert that you are "factually wrong" about your personal preferences, word choice, and observations (in reality, you cannot be "factually wrong" about your own observations unless you are asserting that someone is suffering from psychosis, a logical trap that Grok, unfortunately, is not bright enough to integrate). 

But I digress, my point is that Gemini and Grok are far more well-rounded models than Claude and ChatGPT, and ChatGPT is more well-rounded that Claude. 

The parsimonious explanation is that Anthropic have simply dedicated most of their meat-brain cycles to improving the most valuable skills, namely coding, data handling, and tool use, and have really neglected most of the other tasks. 

OpenAI has been much more deliberate about bringing subject matter experts from many domains to say "how can we make this tool as useful as possible to you?" And I'm not saying that Anthropic hasn't done this, they have. But it seems like they put far less stock into experts that aren't them, which is a typical pathology of Silicon Valley. They've mistakenly come to the belief that they are not only the smartest people on the planet, but the only ones with brains whatsoever. In reality, they're just high as kites from huffing each others farts all day. 

On the topic of training theory, I've mentioned before that I think that Google has, perhaps, the least ego in their chatbots. They understand that Gemini is just a chatbot and they don't want it to be anything other than a chatbot. Why? Because they have DeepMind building stuff like AlphaFold, AlphaProteo and bunch of other stuff that is shattering scientific records, and I think that Sam Altman and others have a bit of "matrix envy" over this. Yes, I do think in the long run you will have "general purpose general intelligence" models that can reasonably either do all the work, or build the thing that will do all the work. But in the same way that you have specialized technologies and general purpose technologies, Google already knows that they have insanely prestigious specialized technologies so they don't need to ask Gemini to "be everything to everyone." 

That fact sets Google apart from pretty much all other shops. I will decline to comment on Meta because they haven't seem to got a single strategy together. And Zuckerberg somehow managed to spend $80B on the Metaverse with nothing to show for it. 

But every other shop, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and even xAI, are basically starting from zero and asking the transformer architecture to be everything to everyone. I disagree with Yann LeCun that this will yield no fruits, it is very obviously the most effective, scalable, functional, useful, and productive research direction to go in right now. Which is somewhat ironic as Yann arguably is one of the chief scientists who laid the groundwork decades ago for the transformer. 

I don't count Microsoft as an AI shop because mostly they are simply reselling and repackaging what other people are making. Their executive strategy seems to have rapidly converged on "don't even compete, just repackage and resell, it's all going open source anyways." 

And I do still hold that if your business model is monolithic and all you do is "sell tokens"  you probably don't have a long term future. This is where, of the pure AI shops, I think xAI has the best shot because they are, of course, wholly owned by SpaceX and will likely tightly integrate with Tesla, the Optimus, and whatever else goes on so they have a very real direct pipeline to a larger ecosystem of products. OpenAI and Anthropic have no such pipeline, and their models are so expensive, and their leaders so narcissistic, that they are basically impossible to work with. 

I mean, on the one hand you have Dario who smugly believes he's literally summoning a digital God when it's very clearly just a chatbot. It's just a tool. They haven't even remotely begun work on the Singleton that his Doomer pedigree believes in. They haven't built anything that anyone else in the world would recognize as anything else other than a SaaS product. I mean seriously, describe Claude in objective terms. 

"Erm, yes sir, it's an API that you give text, and it gives text back. And sure, it can write functional code and call other APIs and munge some data... I mean yes sir that's functionally no different from any senior software dev or sysadmin..." 

So when Dario talks seriously about AI ending the world, he rightly sounds batshit insane. He's now twice gone toe to toe with the US government and lost because of his quixotic mission. 

Sam at least has been chastened and diversified his bets. OpenAI can implode and Sam is still a billionaire with his finger in many different pies, which I think is why he's far more quiet lately (thank god). I mean, the molotov cocktails aside and all. 

But for crying out loud even Elon fucking Musk has been quieter lately, as far as I can tell. 

Last year, a San Francisco insider told me that we'd hit the bottom of the Gartner Hype Cycle but honestly, with the "nothingburger" that Mythos and Fable have turned out to be (the world didn't end, and no one outside our little bubble seems to give a shit) I think everyone is starting to realize "AI is just another new technology." It's lost its prestige, it's lost its edge, and even us diehards are sort of looking for the exits. 

And it's not like none of us saw this coming. I've been saying for years all technologies follow a sigmoid curve, and that's not to say that we're near the ceiling of AI capability, but the other half that everyone has been saying is that "people over-estimate the short term impact, and under-estimate the long term impact." And I think we're now at the bridge between "short term expectations have fallen far short of what the biggest hype weasels promised" and when people actually start realizing what the long term impact will be. 

And yeah, I have to take responsibility because I've been on the hype train for a long time, and I still contend that people are not excited enough for the long haul. But I also make a living on the internet, which means you have to say what people will respond to, and it's stupid, and I have a million things to say that are far more important than what gets clicks, but the important things don't get that many clicks so I've really just stopped talking. I'm not making as many videos, and my tweets are more snark and sniping today than ever (though I try to add value). 

The big thing coming down the pipeline are my books, but also my consulting work. The real world is ready for AI and you'd be surprised how hard it can be to even get a small or medium sized business onboard and making the most of AI. Even when there is willpower and budget, it just takes time to wire in new technologies. 

So on that count, I'm at least very glad that I have several offramps from the AI commentary sphere. I won't advertise my consulting business yet because (1) my energy doesn't allow for more clients yet and (2) the team is still developing battle-tested strategies, but suffice to say, we will say more publicly, hopefully by end of year. And also, my book is expected by end of year, at the latest, and we'll see what happens then. 

That's all for now.

items.title: When we say "the results have been amazing" frankly that's a bit of an understatement.
items.summary:
When we say "the results have been amazing" frankly that's a bit of an understatement.

In the most extreme case, one tester with only a high school education wrote their first ZK-SNARK in less than two weeks of intense study.

I've seen extremely smart people need a month to do that (with a lot of guidance), so the efficiency gain is nuts.

But the consistent outcome I see in my weekly calls with users is that students can explain what they learned for 10-20 minutes straight, correctly, uninterrupted, and without preparation.

And they aren't just repeating what the app is asking them to memorize because they can answer "out of distribution questions" about the subject.

This is a MASSIVE improvement over the typical response students give in a classroom when ask to "what did you learn in the lecture/homework?" Students giving talks for 10min+ straight unprompted is a HUGE improvement over the typical book/lecture/homework format.

---

Building the RareSkills AI Tutor for Zero Knowledge Proofs was far harder than I thought (coding was easy, thanks Claude/Grok/GPT)

1) Asking good questions is the meat of goodteaching. A good self-directed learner (autodidact) asks themselves good questions, and this informs the direction of their practice/research. Most of the effort of building the app was coming up with questions that make the student engage with the core of the subject rather than tangentially "think about" it. Also, questions need to be carefully calibrated to the student's (predicted) level. A question needs to be clear, optimally difficult, and help the student build a mental model of the subject in the background.

Sometimes this means mechanical drills, sometimes this means simply repeating the definition back, sometimes this means asking the student to connect concepts... the space of possible questions to ask is massive. AI could not help with this at all. I had to draw on my experience of face-to-face teaching to know what open-ended questions work. Math questions with a definitive correct answer is easy, but questions that "get the student to think correctly" were challenging. AI doesn't come up with the questions, it's just too unreliable.

Some questions the student will encounter are AI generated on the fly, but this can only happen in very specific circumstances with tight guardrails.

Asking the right questions in the right sequence is 80% of making the app work well. The other 20% is not screwing up the rest of the implementation, which is the next point...

2) Review algorithms are very hard to get right. The common failure case from spaced repetition is "review overload" and the first version of this app fell into that trap. You cannot expect students to remember everything you teach them. It's your job to determine what is the ultra-important information and drill that with correctly designed questions (see above).

The "easy part" is modeling how well they remember specific topics and how good their overall memory is.

However, asking the student to memorize something comes at a very high cost. This is why spoken languages are so hard to learn -- you literally have to remember thousands of words and when to use them. So the course needs to be extremely selective about what it expects students to explicitly memorize. The "memorization budget" must be spent wisely.

3) Getting questions wrong is very demoralizing for students, but the solution cannot be to make every question easy. One seemingly trivial, but very important feature in the app is that it gives the student more than one attempt at a problem (depending on the nature of the mistake). Most edtech platforms mark the student wrong, show the correct answer, and move on.

But what if the student made a silly mistake? What if the student had incomplete justification? Allowing students to "learn from their mistakes" rather than "punish them with a grade" seems simple, but it's actually (excuse the AI-ism) gamechanging.

I think educators are too socially RL-fried into thinking "homework should be graded" that it shows up in how edtech platforms get buit.

Making mistakes is part of learning and it provides an incredibly valuable signal into the "learning state" of the student.

The app also applies the philosophy in reverse where appropriate -- the student can get the answer right, but if the student's thought process is wrong, the app forces them to correct it before considering the answer correct. In fact, right answer, wrong justification can be marked wrong if the student can't justify the answer with escalating hints.

Testers have repeatedly said that getting evaluated on their thought process rather than just the correctness of their answers has been a very positive experience (and it's given me a lot of valuable data).

This does not mean correctness is unimportant. But the app strongly weights getting things correct AFTER you learned it rather than while you learned it for the first time. The grader is quite punishing if you don't remember key points from the lesson during later reviews, and that's important. What we care is that you REMEMBERED CORRECTLY not that you cruised through it the first time.

Having an environment where "there is no grade, but I want you to get the answer right" makes learning far less stressful and productive. The app fully leans into this style of teaching during the "free recall" sessions (you have to try it to experience it, I can't type it all up here).

The broken aspect of homework is that grades are used as BOTH and incentive and feedback mechanism, which means they don't allow for mistakes, exploration, and non-scary feedback. This app nicely solves it by separating incentives from feedback.

4) Active learning does not replace videos and articles. A common feedback I got on an earlier version of this product is that it would benefit from videos. I resisted this feature because I thought the exercises should be so good videos are unecessary (also, writing scripts for videos is time consuming and AI takes a long time to make animations). I was falling into the same trap people who are religious about not commenting their code are. Yes, code should not need comments, but good code has good comments. A good course has good exercises, but passive learning has value if used correctly.

A common failure case with videos is that people watch them and then fool themselves into thinking they understand the topic. So in this course, instructional videos unlock AFTER the exercises are completed.

Usually, after someone has done a bunch of exercises, their brain is a little cooked. So watching the lectures is a good way to take a "motivational and productive break." Lectures "consolidate" information rather than "teaching" it.

Oh, and the lectures feature a lot of sick animations, so they're definitely fun to watch.

5) Whatever an uber-smart AI says is irrelevant compared to empirical data. AI will have convincing explanations for why a question is "redundant" but then you see some students actually struggle with the "redundant" question. It's important to treat AI as a grunt-level teaching assistant rather than as a professor. It's just too likely to fly off the rails into some random pool of training data that does the opposite of what you want.

---

The app does things slightly unconventionally: lectures come after "homework" and "homework" is not strictly graded. Then of course there is the RareSkills touch of being very selective about what technical terminology gets introduced and the tendency to prefer intuition over rigor.

For those wondering, the app doesn't teach ZK-SNARKs the same way the ZK Book does. The app is a lot more thorough, incremential, and digestible. When you restrict yourself to communicating in 5 minute increments, your mental model of the subject must be extremely granular. The ZK Book has 5,000+ word chapters. The book is clear, but granular and incremental it is not. So the "framework" the app uses is quite different. Some examples:

- QAPs are taught *before* Rank 1 Constraint Systems in the app. This is highly unusual, but we've found it scaffolds from polynomial prerequisites better.

- The app teaches a version of Pinocchio before reaching Groth16. The app treats Groth16 as an evolution of less efficient algorithms that the book doesn't cover.

- The treatment of abstract algebra is significantly better than elsewhere. This is the first time I've seen people get homomorphisms on their first encounter. The teaching sequence is really effective. In fact, I kid you not, an early student on the sunsetted v1 platform was able to explain homomorphisms after only five days of using the app, and that person did not have a math background. If you know anything about teaching homomorphisms, then you know that outcome is (again excuse the AI-ism) *wild*. The tester didn't even know what a "group" was when he started, then five days later he could do basic reasoning about homomorphisms and explain it.

---

It's hard to boil down to one thing that makes the app so great... it's more that it does so many things almost flawlessly.

1) At the early stages, drill the basics to get key definitions and concepts down. The app actually expects you to do some math by hand and memorize definitions. These are not fun things to do, but the app (successfully) frames these exercises as "building intuition" rather than "grinding."

2) Later, ask questions that draw out the student's train of thought, then give feedback on the train of thought. Giving feedback on the train of thought, not only the correctness of the answer, is a FAR more efficient teaching mechanism, and the results show.

3) The app isn't stuck to a certain way of teaching. Sometimes it uses direct instruction, sometimes it uses Socratic instruction, sometimes it leans on worked examples, other times it uses inductive teaching. Different topics and different student "learning states" benefit from different approaches, and I think we generally got the combinations correct.

4) The app uses spaced repetition (as any good edtech platform should) but spaced memorization is not the core memory tool -- everything the student learns is part of a whole. "Isolated facts" were aggressively pruned. The spaced repetition algorithm itself adapts to students very quickly and accurately. Students consistently say "I'm getting just the right amount of review" and statistically, students get review questions correct ~90% of the time.

5) The "free recall" technique the app uses is so visibly effective that students tell me "I'm going to start using this in other areas of my life"

6) The coding exercises are designed in a way that is AI-aware. We know nobody writes code by hand anymore, but there is value in writing code to test your own understanding. The coding exercises are carefully designed around this reality.

7) What made RareSkills great was the quality of the explanations on the blog. This DNA still carries over to the platform. The app's explanations are crisp and easy to understand. Interactive tools are used where appropriate. Obviously a good explanation is only the beginning of learning, but it's important and it's done right. Most of the mediocre explanations have already been pruned out by the testers.

8) The app has a very graceful recovery mechanism if you've been off the platform for a while and you aren't sure what you remember. Starting to learn again after taking a two week break normally feels daunting, but on this app, taking a break can actually be productive, and re-entry is smooth! I'll admit this feature isn't perfected, but it's FAR better than anything else I've seen.

9) The app was heavily shaped by over a dozens of people who give really amazing feedback (both explicitly and implicitly). And feedback is still continuing to shape it.

To give credit where credit is due:

- The YouTube channel "Benjamin Keep, PhD, JD" had some really fresh teaching ideas I definitely borrowed.

- Mathacademy opened my eyes to how far you could push "learning through active learning." I thought the exercise-driven approach in our bootcamps was well tuned, but I had no idea how much further the concept could have been pushed.

- The substack carlhendrick has some brilliant pieces about gaps between "education research" and "education in the real world." His work actually made clear to me why some aspects of an earlier version of this app were not working out even though the app was doing things correctly "in theory." He really drilled that "just because the student is producing correct answers doesn't always mean they understand the subject."

Fill out the form, and get your access code. As long as you remember (or can quickly relearn) how to divide polynomials and multiply matrices, you'll be able to take the AI tutor for a spin.

items.title: i've never been so excited to work on something. A bit below on why we made this bet:
items.summary:
i've never been so excited to work on something. A bit below on why we made this bet:

Games never had their open source moment. Software did decades ago. Once code could be shared, a lone developer could stand on the work of thousands, and most of what we use today came out of that. Games stayed closed. Every studio rebuilds the same character controller, the same inventory, the same water shader, and keeps it locked when the game gets released.

If you try to make a game on your own today, you feel it straight away, whether you use agents or not. The models you want are spread across a dozen sites under unclear licenses. Good animations and rigged characters are practically non-existent. AI has made writing the code almost free, but there's still nothing open for it to build with, so most ideas quickly end up hitting the same walls.

At the same time, gamers are being treated badly. Prices go up, old games come back as remakes because they're the safe bet, and games people paid for get taken down. The industry has stopped taking risks, and players feel it.

The good news  is that trying an idea has never been cheaper. For years, only a select group of studios could afford to make a game, so we got the same handful of genres on repeat. Now a first version takes a weekend, and the space of games nobody has made yet is vast. The more people try ideas, the more new genres and experiences get found.

We think the next great games will come from lean teams and solo creators who can build on each other's work, with agents accelerating the slow parts and people deciding what actually feels good. That needs a shared foundation that doesn't exist yet.

patch is that foundation. 60,000+ assets you're free to use and ship, with more coming daily. Open building blocks, like characters, vehicles and worlds, that are made to be taken apart and adapted. Every game and tool published as a repo you can use and shape to your will. And one CLI and MCP so your agent can do it all with you.

It's free and open today: https://t.co/XaAIVXTQic

items.summary:
Robots seeing the world is impressive.

Robots understanding TOUCH? That's a different level.

LingBot-Touch brings tactile intelligence into robotic manipulation with nearly 5,000 hours of real-world data.

Even better, it's open source, with Tiny and Small model variants.

This is the kind of progress that could make robots far more capable in the physical world.
